problem: Multi-view ALFRED agents simply concatenate view features and use a single flat action classifier. Separately, benchmarks with a private test set encourage model selection on one unseen validation set, and it is unclear whether validation gains carry over to the unseen test set.
motivation: ALFRED needs both navigation and manipulation, and non-SLAM agents lag behind map-based ones. The authors built a stronger multi-view model that beat baselines on unseen validation but not on unseen test, so they use it to show that a single unseen validation set can mislead model selection.
key_idea: Match each view's fused embedding to the embedding of the action that would produce it (view-action matching), add an action-type gate that separates navigation from manipulation actions, and use the resulting validation-to-test gap to argue that unseen validation performance does not guarantee generalization.
insight: The ablation on unseen validation shows steady gains (SR 4.7 to 9.3 to 11.8 to 13.8), but the gap between validation and test is larger than those gains. The full model is best on validation (13.8) yet worse on test (8.57) than ABP (15.43), while ABP shows the reverse trend. Seed variance is about 3% SR, so selecting the best model on one unseen validation set can overfit to that set's visual differences.
method: Base model: LXMERT with 2 language and 2 cross-modal layers, hidden size 768. Faster R-CNN region features (pretrained on AI2-THOR, following Pashevich et al.) are average-pooled, combined with action-history features by a linear layer, then fused with language through cross-modal attention.
Wide view: five views (front, left, right, up, down) are each processed to give per-view features V_i, instead of a single front view.

View-Action Matching: a feedforward network scores each view feature V_i against the embedding A_i of the action that generates that view, giving matching scores M_i. This is an analogue of viewpoint selection that works despite AI2-THOR's irreversible actions.

Action-Type Gate: a linear layer over all view features predicts weights favoring actions of the ground-truth type (navigation vs non-navigation). The weights multiply M_i pointwise and the highest-scoring action is chosen.
Loss: cross-entropy for actions (teacher forcing) and object type. Training uses AdamW with learning rate 1e-5, and model selection uses SR on the unseen validation split.

setting.backbone: LXMERT-based transformer (trained on ALFRED), Faster R-CNN visual features
setting.training_data: ALFRED train split trajectories with hierarchical language instructions; no extra data
setting.observation: egocentric RGB from 5 views (front, left, right, up, down) plus language instructions and action history
setting.action_space: discrete AI2-THOR navigation and manipulation actions plus object segmentation mask

numbers.method: Ours (full: wide view + view-action matching + action-type gate)

numbers_note: ALFRED is not in the canonical benchmark list, so it is labelled 'ALFRED' as printed by the paper. The test-seen row uses a split name outside the given list. Ablation SRs on val-unseen (4.7, 9.3, 11.8, 13.8) are in Table 1 and not repeated as separate entries.
results: On unseen validation, the full model reaches SR 13.8 / GC 28.1, beating ABP (12.55) and LWIT (9.70). On unseen test, it gets SR 8.57 versus ABP's 15.43 and roughly matches LWIT's 8.37, so the validation lead does not carry over.
limitations: Test performance is below the strongest baseline (ABP), so the proposed modules give no demonstrated test-set gain.
The overfitting-to-validation explanation is a hypothesis; no multi-seed or multi-split experiments confirm it, and seed variance (~3%) is only mentioned briefly.
Only non-SLAM multi-view baselines are compared, and the study covers a single benchmark, ALFRED.
